docs.title: Welcome to Evolution for Everyone!
docs.text:
We are outreach organization making evolutionnary biology more accessible to students and scientists across the world!

🍄 Our mission is to promote equitable access to knowledge, resources and opportunities in evolutionary biology, empowering equity-deserving students to become scientists.

🦋 We offer free workshops in universities! if you are interested in having a workshop at your university, please reach out at leticiamagpali@dal.ca

🦋 You can also learn by yourself right here! To acess all our workshops tutorials, data and materials, as well as outside resources, check our Learning tab.

🦋 If you are a collaborator, find our project roadmap here.

🦋 Bioinformatics for Everyone has received funding and support from the following organizations:

Digital Alliance of Canada's EDIA Champions Program OLS Open Seeds Mentoring and Training Program

Register for the Bioinformatics for Beginners worskhop series here!

docs.text: 🦋 Knowledge is plural and that's beautiful! 🦋 Knowledge should be open, equitably shared and accessible to everyone (whenever possible) 🦋 Science should be inclusive, acessible and collaborative

docs.title: 🍄 What is Bioinformatics?
docs.text:
Info

In simple terms, Bioinformatics is using computers and programing languages to analyse biological data You can analyse a lot of different data using bioinformatics, such as genetic sequences, measurements taken in the field, or the results of an experiment you did at the lab 🧬

(By the end of our course, you will understand this joke o/)

docs.title: 🍄 Why Bioinformatics workshops?
docs.text: Bioinformatics is becoming increasignly important in every field of biology, from genomics and biochemestry to behavioral ecology and conservation. Bioinformatic tools increase our ability to colect, store and process large amounts of data At the same time, biologists (you and me!) are not properly trained to use computational tools, and this lack of training has many reasons: * bioinformatic tools and methods are oftentimes complicated for first time users, and require a lot of training * a lot of universities still don't offer bioinformatics courses in the biology program * taking courses on your own can be very expensive and time consuming (PS: you can learn how to program online in various languages - click here for a list of free/afordable courses - but the courses to learn how to run computational analyses are scarse and expensive)

docs.title: Tutorial 0 - Introduction to command line and bash
1. Opening the terminal
docs.text:
🍄 What is the terminal?

The terminal is a text-based interface where you communicate with your computer by typing commands. To talk with the computer, the terminal uses a programming language. The most popular terminal languages in bioinformatics are bash and zsh.

You can use the terminal to do anything you normally do in your computer! (for example, running programs, creating, editing and accessing files and folders.)

Tip

What's so special about the terminal? It allows you to run a lot of programs that don't have a graphic interface!

Many programs we use for analysis in evolutionary biology don't have a graphic interface - that means they don't have an app, a screen or clickable icons, and we have to interact with them using only programming language.

🍄 Where do I find the terminal?

The terminal looks just like another app on your computer - but it will change slightly depending on the operating system you are on (Linux, MacOS or Windows). Follow the instructions below according to your system:

→ For MacOS/Linux users

  • You can locate the terminal in the list of apps (launchpad) of your computer,
  • or use the search option by pressing the F4 key (which should have an eyeglass 🔍 icon) and then typing terminal into the search box.
  • The terminal icon looks like a black box with a < and a -, like this:

→ For Windows users

  • The Windows native terminal does not work with bash or zsh, so it's not suitable for our needs.
  • When working with Windows computers, we need to install the Linux system to get access to the terminal.
  • For that, follow this written tutorial, or this video tutorial.

🐞 Once you have located the terminal on your computer, go ahead and open it! It should look like a black window with some text at the top, like this:

docs.title: 2. The structure of the terminal
docs.text:
Every time you open your terminal, you will see the following information at the top left corner:

user@computer directory % # if you are using MacOS

user@computer:directory$ # if you are using Linux/Unix

Tip

This line is called the prompt, and it means the computer is ready to accept a command from you - in other words, it's prompting you.

🍄 Now let's break down the elements of the prompt:

1️⃣ user and computer are the names you set up for yourself and your computer For example, my user name is letixa and my computer name is eujenio. You can set them to anything you want!

2️⃣ directory is the folder you are currently in (computer people use this fancy name directory, which really just means folder).

  • Some operating systems (OS) will only show the name of the directory, while others will show the whole path to that directory.
  • When you open your terminal, the directory will show as ~. This is a path symbol that represents your HOME directory.

3️⃣ $ or % is a prompt symbol, indicating that the terminal is waiting for a command. When you see this symbol, it means it's ok to type stuff on the terminal!

What about the (base) that shows on my screenshot? This is to indicate which environment you are in - we will see more details about that in the future.

docs.title: 3. Using command-line (bash) in the terminal
docs.text:
Now we are ready to begin typing commands from inside our terminal! For the next steps, you will see a series of commands that you will type on your terminal, in front of the % or $ sign, and then hit Enter to run. Some commands will require additional words in front of them, others won't.

Before getting started, rememeber: terminal commands are case-sensitive! So if you type ls it will work, but if you type LS, it wont't.

Here's a cheat-sheet for the most popular commands:

List of commands

  • pwd — Print working directory: shows the directory you are in right now.
  • ls — List: lists all the contents of a directory (files and subdirectories).
  • cd — Change directory: moves to a different directory through the path you indicate.
  • mkdir — Make directory: creates a new directory.
  • nano — Text editor for creating and editing text files.
  • cat — Concatenate: displays the contents of a file or files.
  • mv — Move: moves or renames files or directories.
  • clear - Clear: refreshes your screen clearing everything in it.

docs.title: 🍄 Moving between different directories
docs.text:
🐞 First, let's find out where we are (aka our working directory). Type pwd in your prompt, then hit Enter. You should see a set of words separated by slashes show up in the next line, like in the example below:

(base) letixa@eugenio ~ % pwd
/Users/letixa

This line represents the complete pathway to the directory (folder) you are currently in.

In my case, I am in my home directory, located at /Users/letixa.

🐞 What files are inside my home directory? We can use ls to find out! Type ls in your prompt, then hit Enter. The screen will show a bunch of words - these are the names of all folders and files you have inside your home directory.

(base) letixa@eugenio ~ % ls
Applications            Library                 Public
Desktop                 Mesquite_Support_Files  Zotero
Documents               Movies                  src
Downloads               Music                   zsh-syntax-highlighting
Google Drive            Pictures

🐞 Now let's go to the directory where we want to work! Choose a folder in your home to start organizing your tutorial files. Then, navigate to that folder using cd followed by the folder name. For example, I want to go to my Documents directory, which is inside my home directory:

(base) letixa@eugenio ~ % cd Documents
(base) letixa@eugenio Documents %

Note that the directory on your prompt has now changed from ~ to the name of the directory you just entered (in my case, Documents). Now you are inside Documents!

🐞 What if I want to go to a folder that's inside another folder? In that case, if you try to just type the name of the folder, the computer won't know where to go. You need to use cd along with the complete path to that folder starting from your current location, like this:

(base) letixa@eugenio ~ % cd Documents/work
(base) letixa@eugenio work %
In this example, I went to the directory work, which is inside Documents. If I had just used cd work, I would get an error like this:

(base) letixa@eugenio ~ % cd work
cd: no such file or directory: work

In this error, the computer is saying "there's nothing called work here". Because you are typing the command from your home, and your work directory is not inside home (it is inside home Documents).

And here we get to an important terminal lesson:

A command on the terminal only works if you are running it from the correct location! That basically means that:

  • If the file or folder targeted by your command is located where you are, you can just type [command] [space] [name of file/folder].
  • However, if your target is in a different location, your command needs to include the path to that file or folder. We will see many examples of this later!

docs.title: 🍄 Creating directories and files
docs.text:
Now that you are in the right location to store your tutorials, let's start making some folders to keep things organized!

🐞 Create a master directory

First, we'll make a master folder to contain everything related to our tutorials. For that, enter the mkdir command followed by the name you wish to give your folder, like this:

mkdir tutorials

Now enter ls, to check if the folder was created. You should see it showing up in your screen like this:

(base) letixa@eugenio Documents % ls
tutorials

You may have other folders in there as well - as long as you see the name of the folder you just created, it's all good! Now go inside our tutorials directory by using:

cd tutorials

and list what's inside it using ls. You should get an empty line, because the folder is empty:

(base) letixa@eugenio tutorials % ls
(base) letixa@eugenio tutorials %

Tip

Using TAB as autocomplete

Instead of typing a full word, you can type only the first letter(s) and use TAB to autocomplete. For example, for the cd command above, you can type cd t + TAB, and it will autocomplete to cd tutorials.

If you have another folder that begins with t, it will show you the possible options; keep hitting TAB to switch between them and press Enter when you find the right one.

What if you want to go back to your original folder? You can also use cd, followed by ../, which means "the folder before this one":

cd ../
This tells your computer to go to the folder immediately before the one you're at right now.

🐞 Create a README file

Next, let's use the command nano to create a README.txt file:

nano README.txt
As soon as you enter this command, you should see an empty black screen. It's all good! This is how an empty document looks in your terminal. You can type anything on it and it will be saved as a text file! So let's do it:

  • Type a title for your README file (for example, BIOINFORMATICS TUTORIALS).
  • Then use Ctrl + X, followed by Y and Enter to exit and save the file.

Now, let's enter ls to see what's inside your tutorials folder. You should see a result like this:

(base) letixa@eugenio Documents % ls
README.txt
You can come back to re-edit this file at any time, by entering nano README.txt, typing new lines below the title and then saving the document. To learn more about the nano command and how to use it, check out this video tutorial!

🐞 What if I want to see what's written in my file? To take a look at any text file, we can use the command cat, followed by the file name. Type cat README.txt on your terminal and hit Enter. The terminal will display the content of your file, like this:

(base) letixa@eugenio Documents % cat README.txt
BIOINFORMATICS TUTORIALS
The only thing written on your file is the title - so that's what the terminal will show!

Note

To take this lesson further, try writing the content of your README file! For more information on how to write a README file, check this webpage.

docs.title: 🍄 Changing and moving files
docs.text:
Can I change the name and location of a file?

Yes you can! The mv command allows you to do both. Let's check it out:

🐞 Renaming a file:

Let's assume you wanted to change the name of your README file to README_tutorials.txt, to make it more specific. You can do that by entering mv followed by the old name, then the new name, like this:

mv README.txt README_tutorials.txt

And, to check if the command worked, let's use ls:

(base) letixa@eugenio tutorials % ls
README_tutorials.txt
Looks good!

🐞 Moving a file:

Let's say you want the README.txt file to be inside tutorials, instead of Documents. Creating a file in the wrong folder is a very common mistake, so how can we correct it? From inside Documents, we can enter mv followed by the file name and the new location, like this:

(base) letixa@eugenio Documents % mv README.txt tutorials

You can now navigate to tutorials and check if README.txt is there, like this:

(base) letixa@eugenio Documents % cd tutorials
(base) letixa@eugenio tutorials % ls
README.txt

Success!

docs.title: 4. Challenge: creating a folder structure
docs.text:
Every bioinformatician needs to be organized! In this challenge, we will create folders to store data, notes and exercises for our tutorials. Try to type the command by yourself first, then open the toggle to check.

(Before starting, make sure you are inside the tutorials folder.)

🐞 Create a directory named sandbox

A sandbox is a place where we can test everything without compromising our analysis. It's always good to have one!

Click to check command 
mkdir sandbox

🐞 Create one directory for each tutorial.

Suggestion of name: tutorial_1, tutorial_2, etc. (Always use _ instead of spaces, because spaces don't go well in the terminal.)

Click to check command

There are two ways you can do this:

  • Use mkdir individually for each folder, or
  • Create all folders at once:
mkdir tutorial_1 tutorial_2 tutorial_3 tutorial_4 tutorial_5 tutorial_6

Now when you list the content of your master folder, you should see something like this:

(base) letixa@eugenio tutorials % ls
README.txt tutorial_1 tutorial_3 tutorial_5
sandbox    tutorial_2 tutorial_4 tutorial_6

Warning

Got an error after typing a command?

Here's a few things you can check before telling your computer to go to %@#!

  • Are you in the right folder?
  • Did you type the right pathways for the input options?
  • Did you spell everything right? No typos?

Remember: Computers are really dumb! You have to tell them exactly what you want.

docs.title: Tutorial 1 - Setting up your workspace
docs.text:
Before you get started in the fantastical world of bioinformatics and molecular evolution, there's a few programs your computer needs first. We are going to install those one by one.

Some of the programs we will install are the regular kind of download that we are all used to, but others require the command-line, which you have already learned about in Tutorial 0.

docs.title: Installing alignment visualizing tools
docs.text:
In Tutorial 3, we will visualize sequence alignments. Below are the links to the most commonly used free apps for alignment visualization:

  • Aliview
  • Jalview
  • Seaview

Our tutorial follows Aliview, but you're welcome to try them all, and choose your preferred one!

docs.title: Installing Conda
docs.text:
Conda is an environment and software manager. It is required to install and run NCBI datasets, which you will do next. Install conda here. Don't forget to follow the right instructions for your operational system!

Checkpoint

For the next steps, open up your terminal app (it's the black window app, you learned about it in Tutorial 0.)

docs.title: Command-line installation - instructions
docs.text:
As we saw on Tutorial 0, command-line is a way to talk to your computer using written commands inside an app called terminal. The next software we will install don't have a graphic interface, so we need to download them using the command-line.

For each software installation, you will do the same actions, described below:

With your terminal open on one side of the screen, and this tutorial on the other:

  • Locate the command you need to copy from the tutorial. Commands are always inside a grey text box.
  • Select the entire command (everything inside the grey box) and copy it.
  • Paste the copied command in your terminal prompt.
  • Hit Enter; this will run the command.

Important

The terminal will be full of scrolling text for a few seconds/minutes. That's ok! Just leave it there, and don't type anything else until you see the prompt is accepting commands again.

Remember: how do we know the prompt is accepting commands? It will show an empty line that has only your user and computer name, like this: 

user@computer ~ %

  • Once an installation is complete, you can begin another the same way.

docs.title: Installing Xcode command-line tools (for mac users)
docs.text:
This package contains language compilers and other tools that are necessary to install most of our other software. So let's get this done first!

xcode-select --install

docs.title: Installing NCBI datasets
docs.text:
• Create conda environment: conda create -n ncbi_datasets

  • Activate conda environment: conda activate ncbi_datasets

  • Install the datasets conda package: conda install -c conda-forge ncbi-datasets-cli

docs.title: Installing Git
docs.text:
Git is a repository manager. It helps us keep track of the changes we make in our files over time, and it's great for collaborative work.

MacOS: After you installed Xcode, you should have Git automatically! So all we need is to do a quick check:

git --version
This command will tell you the version of Git you have currently installed. If it runs, it means the installing worked!

Windows/Linux:

Linux has a native function called apt-get install that you can use to get a lot of programs. Let's use it to get Git:

sudo apt-get install git-all

docs.title: Installing Homebrew (for macOS silicon only)
docs.text: Homebrew is a package manager for macOS silicon (i.e., the newer Macbooks with the Apple M1-M4 chips) that is very useful for installing and maintaing "command-line only" programs. It will make it easier for us to install all sorts of other software and packages! If you have an older Macbook, don't worry about this - just skip to the next section. We'll follow the instructions on this page to install Homebrew.

docs.title: MAFFT
docs.text:
1. macOS (silicon)

    brew install mafft

  2. macOS (intel) 

    conda create -n mafft
conda activate mafft
conda install bioconda::mafft

  3. Windows/Linux users

    sudo apt update
sudo apt install mafft

docs.title: IQtree
docs.text:
1. macOS (silicon)

    brew install iqtree3

  2. macOS (intel)

    conda create -n iqtree
conda activate iqtree
conda install bioconda::iqtree

  3. Windows/Linux users 

    sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install iqtree

docs.title: PAML
docs.text:
1. macOS users

    brew install paml

  2. macOS (intel) and Windows/Linux:

    conda create -n paml
conda activate paml
conda install bioconda::paml

docs.title: 1. Server? What is that?
docs.text:
If you are in a bioinformatics lab, you will probably have to work on a server at some point. When I first joined a lab as an undergraduate, server was this ethereal, mysterious word for a parallel universe I could access from my computer to run analyses. Back then, I had so many unanswered questions:

  • What is a server?
  • How does it look like?
  • What is it made of?
  • Where does it stay?
  • Why do we need them?

Let's start this tutorial by answering those questions:

docs.title: 🍄 What is a server?
docs.text:
A server is a computer, or a collection of computers working together, that provides resources such as processing power, storage, or software. We use servers for the same reason people work together to solve complex problems: one computer may be enough for some tasks, while others need more computing power.

A small server can be just a few computers in a research office, while a large server can look like this:

docs.title: 🍄 What's cool about a server?
docs.text:
• Servers are often more powerful than personal computers, so they can store more data, process it faster, and handle more complicated problems.
  • You can run software on a server using its computing resources, including analyses that your laptop might not be able to handle.
  • A process running on a server can continue after you disconnect from it, if it was started in a way that keeps it running.
  • A server administrator may install and maintain software for the research group.

That sounds awesome! How do I access a server?

Let's learn more in the next section.

docs.title: 2. Accessing a server
docs.text:
Our computers can connect to a server over the internet using the ssh (Secure Shell) command in a terminal. To connect, you need the server's address and your username. Depending on how the server is configured, you may also need a port number, a password, an SSH key, or multi-factor authentication.

The general command is:

ssh -p [port] [username]@[server]

The -p [port] part is only needed if the server uses a non-default SSH port. After you enter the command, you may be asked to authenticate.

docs.title: 🍄 The Alliance servers
docs.text:
The Digital Research Alliance of Canada has a collection of servers available to researchers affiliated with Canadian institutions: Beluga, Cedar, Graham, Narval, and Niagara.

🐞 Registering for an Alliance server account

To access the Alliance servers, first register for an account with the Alliance's CCDB.

  • If you are a principal investigator (PI), you can apply directly for an account.
  • If you are a student or research-group member, your supervisor must have an account to sponsor your application at no cost.

🐞 Setting up your server account

Once your application has been approved (usually within 1–2 business days), follow the setup instructions for:

  1. Multi-factor authentication
  2. SSH keys (recommended)
  3. For Niagara, the opt-in page. Open the page and click the join button. Check the Alliance documentation for current requirements for other servers.

🐞 Logging in to your account

Use the login command provided by the Alliance for your selected server. For example:

ssh [username]@[server].alliancecan.ca

Replace [username] and [server] with your account and server details. The exact login method may differ depending on the server's authentication requirements.

docs.title: 🍄 The Awarnach server
docs.text:
The Bielawski Group's server is called Awarnach. Read the story behind its name. It is a cluster—a group of computers working together—located in Joe's office. It centralizes data, information, and software for the lab's research projects.

To log in:

  1. Open a terminal.
  2. Run the ssh command with the server's address and your username. The server address is awarnach.mathstat.dal.ca, the port is 22, and each user has a unique username.

For example, if your username is leticiamagpali, the command is:

ssh -p 22 leticiamagpali@awarnach.mathstat.dal.ca

📍 Note: The server administrator sets up your account. Ask your supervisor how to get access and who to contact for troubleshooting.

🍄 Let's practice!

Log in to Awarnach using the ssh command and the account details provided to you. When you type a password, nothing appears on the screen. Type it once, then press Enter.

After a successful login, your screen should look like this:

How do I exit the server?

Type exit at the prompt and press Enter. You should see a message confirming that you disconnected:

logout
Connection to awarnach.mathstat.dal.ca closed.

How do I change my password?

If password changes are enabled on your server, run passwd at the terminal prompt. It will ask for your current password and then your new password.

Warning

Passwords do not appear on the screen while you type them. Enter each password once, then press Enter.

docs.title: 3. Transferring files between the server and your computer
docs.text:
When you work on a server, the files you create are stored on the server, not on your personal computer. To use those files with programs on your computer, you may need to transfer them first.

You can transfer files using the command line or a graphical application such as FileZilla.

docs.title: 🍄 Transferring files via command line
docs.text:
Use the scp command in a terminal on your computer to copy files between your computer and the server.

  1. Open a terminal on your computer.
  2. Choose the command for the direction you want to copy, replacing the placeholders with the correct paths and account details.

From the server to your computer

scp [username]@[server]:/path/to/remote/file /path/to/local/destination/

From your computer to the server

scp /path/to/local/file [username]@[server]:/path/to/remote/destination/

To copy a directory and everything inside it, add the -r option after scp. For example:

scp -r tutorials [username]@[server]:/path/to/remote/destination/

Tip

Use pwd to find the current directory's full path. Run it on the server for a remote path, or in a terminal on your computer for a local path.

docs.title: 🍄 Transferring files with FileZilla
docs.text:
FileZilla is an application that lets you transfer files between your computer and a server using a graphical interface. It can be useful when you want to drag and drop files instead of entering commands.

  1. Download FileZilla Client.
  2. Open FileZilla and enter the server host, username, password or other authentication details, and port. For Awarnach's details, see The Awarnach server.

  3. Click Quickconnect. Your server's folders should appear on the right side of the window.

  4. Drag and drop files from the left side (your computer) to the right side (the server). You can navigate through folders on both sides.

docs.title: 4. Challenge: transferring your master folder to the server
docs.text:
Remember the master folder you created in Tutorial 1 (tutorials)? Your task is to transfer a copy of it to your home folder on the server. Use scp or FileZilla—whichever you prefer!

After you try, open this step-by-step guide

To use scp, I usually have two terminal windows open: one for commands on my computer and one connected to the server. This makes it easier to look up and copy paths.

To copy the tutorials folder from my computer to the server, I need:

  • The path to the folder on my computer.
  • The destination path on the server.

To find the destination path, go to the chosen folder in the server terminal and run pwd:

cd bioinfo4everyone
pwd

In this example, the path is /home/leticiamagpali/bioinfo4everyone.

On your computer, navigate to the directory that contains the tutorials folder. If you created it in Documents, run:

cd ~/Documents

Then copy the folder to the server, replacing the username and destination path with your own:

scp -r tutorials [username]@awarnach.mathstat.dal.ca:/home/[username]/bioinfo4everyone/

docs.title: 1. What do genomic sequences look like on my computer?
docs.text:
A genomic sequence is any sequence that has been extracted from a genome. 🐞 It could be a gene, a protein, or a non-coding element (like a regulatory region).

These sequences are often saved as text files in different formats. One of the most common formats for evolutionary analyses is FASTA.

FASTA format

A FASTA file is made up of two elements:

  • Header: A line at the beginning of a sequence that tells you about it. The header starts with > followed by descriptive text.
  • Sequence: The nucleotides or amino acids that make up the gene, protein, or non-coding element. The sequence starts on the line immediately below the header and is usually wrapped every 60–80 characters.
>XM_019925131.2:314-2584 PREDICTED: Tursiops truncatus forkhead box P2 (FOXP2), mRNA
ATGATGCAGGAATCTGCGACAGAGACAATAAGCAACAGTTCAATGAATCAAAATGGAATGAGCACTCTAA
GCAGCCAATTAGATGCTGGCAGCAGAGATGGAAGATCAAGTGGTGACACCAGCTCTGAAGTAAGCACAGT

docs.title: 2. Downloading genomic sequences
docs.text:
In our tutorials, we will analyze the coding sequences of the FOXP2 gene.

  • Our goal is to investigate how FOXP2 evolved in mammals that are capable of vocal learning (like us!).
  • First, we need to obtain our data set: a collection of FOXP2 sequences for different mammal species.
  • We will download these sequences from NCBI, one of the most widely used genomic databases.

There are two main ways to download these sequences from NCBI:

  • Use the graphical interface on the NCBI website.
  • Use the command line in your terminal.

We will start with the graphical interface. Then, we will learn about the command-line version, which is essential if you are interested in working with coding sequences.

The NCBI website is always changing, so it might look slightly different from the tutorial's images.

docs.title: 🍄 Downloading sequences from NCBI Nucleotide
docs.text:
1. Go to the NCBI Datasets Gene page.

  2. On the search bar, type FOXP2 under Gene symbol and select Mammalia under Taxon, then hit Search.

  3. Select 10 species you want to download by clicking the empty box beside each name. Which species to select? Any one is ok, we are just practicing!

  4. Select Download, then click on Download package.

  5. A Download package window will pop up. Make sure that CDS (FASTA) and Protein sequences (FASTA) are selected. These two options will give you the coding sequences and proteins for the gene. Hit Download.

  6. On your downloads, look for a folder called ncbi_dataset.zip; click it to unzip.

    • This folder has the following structure: ncbi_dataset > ncbi_dataset > data (yes, two folders with the same name). Click through the folders until you reach data.
    • Inside data, you will find 2 files: cds.faa and protein.faa. Save these files in your tutorial_3 folder.

docs.title: 🍄 Pause for a deep breath
docs.text: Brace yourself and take a deep breath. Things will get a little more complicated, but it's nothing you can't master with practice!

docs.title: 🍄 Downloading sequences using command-line
docs.text:
We will now learn how to download genomic sequences using the command line. More specifically, we will download a set of coding sequences (the part of the gene that is translated into a protein) for the gene FOXP2.

This workflow was adapted from NCBI's tutorial: Get one protein per gene from a set of orthologs. Feel free to check it out for more details!

🐞 Our goal is to download one sequence of FOXP2 for each species.

Why just one sequence?

Many genes undergo alternative splicing and have multiple transcript variants (mRNA isoforms). These transcripts come from the same gene, but their coding sequences and lengths can differ.

Many comparative genomic studies use one sequence per gene. A common approach is to select the longest transcript, although the longest transcript is not necessarily the best representative of the complete coding sequence in every case.

  1. Activate the environment where ncbi_datasets is installed:

    source activate ncbi_datasets

  2. From your tutorials folder, navigate to tutorial_3 using cd followed by the path to the folder. 

    cd tutorial_3

  3. We will now download the longest FOXP2 transcript for each species. For the steps below, copy and paste the commands into your terminal and press Enter. Don't forget to read each command to understand what it does!

🐛 This part can be challenging for beginners, so each completed step unlocks a celebratory cat GIF. You got this!

docs.title: 🐞 Getting FOXP2 metadata
docs.text:
We will use the datasets summary command to retrieve metadata about our FOXP2 sequences. We'll use this metadata to figure out which transcript is the longest.

What is metadata?

Metadata is information that provides context about the data. For NCBI sequences, it can include:

  • Common gene name
  • Gene ID (an identifier unique to each gene)
  • Species or taxon name
  • Sequence accession number
  • Sequence length

We can donwload the metadata in two ways: by providing the gene name OR the accession numbers (a unique record number) of the sequences we want to download.

By gene name We are going to use the command below to get every record of FOXP2 for humans and other mammals. Note how the command is built:

  • First, we say we want the summary - which is a data report - and we specify FOXP2 as our target gene with gene symbol
  • Then, we pass 4 options into the command:
    • taxon: the species we want as our reference. 9606 is human (it's safer to use numbers rather than names here)
    • ortholog: the group for which we will download FOXP2 orthologs (same gene for different species), based on our reference species. 40674 is Mammals
    • report product: the type of report we want. In this case, we want the product, which contains the transcript information we need.
    • as-json-lines: the format we want our report in (has to be json because of the next command)
  • What about the backslash (\)? That means a line break - it allows us to write in many lines without breaking the command.
datasets summary gene symbol FOXP2 \
    --taxon 9606 \
    --ortholog 40674 \
    --report product \
    --as-json-lines > foxp2_orthologs.jsonl

By accession number Another way is to download sequences by accession number. This is useful if you already have a list of species you want to download and know their accession numbers from NCBI, for example:

  • Human (Homo sapiens) | NM_014491.4
  • Chimpanzee (Pan troglodytes) | XM_063813769.1
  • Cow (Bos taurus) | NM_001205569.3
  • Bottlenose dolphin (Tursiops truncatus) | XM_019925131.2
  • Killer whale (Orcinus orca) | XM_049715204.1
  • Harbor seal (Phoca vitulina) | XM_032401732.1
  • Dog (Canis lupus familiaris) | XM_038439870.1
  • Little brown bat (Myotis lucifugus) | XM_023760067.1
  • African elephant (Loxodonta africana) | XM_023544567.1
  • Manatee (Trichechus manatus latirostris) | XM_004382567.2

Let's download the sequences for these species:

    datasets summary gene accession \
    NM_014491.4 XM_063813769.1 NM_001205569.3 XM_019925131.2 XM_049715204.1 XM_032401732.1 XM_038439870.1 XM_023760067.1 XM_023544567.1 XM_004382567.2 \
    --report product --as-json-lines > foxp2_orthologs2.jsonl
Well done! Click to unlock celebratory cat #1

docs.title: 🐞 Extracting information about sequence length
docs.text:
We will use the dataformat command to extract the Gene Product Report from our JSON Lines file and convert it into a readable table in TSV format. This report contains information about FOXP2 transcripts and proteins. The --fields option specifies which information to include in the table, such as gene ID, symbol, and transcript length.

dataformat tsv gene-product \
--inputfile foxp2_orthologs.jsonl \
--fields gene-id,tax-name,symbol,transcript-accession,transcript-length,transcript-protein-accession,transcript-protein-length > transcript_protein.tsv

Let's take a look at this table using head, which displays the first 10 lines of a file. It's useful for taking a quick look at long files.

head transcript_protein.tsv

The beginning of your table should look like this:

📍 Let's break down this table:

  • The first line contains the column headers: gene ID, taxonomic name, symbol, transcript accession, transcript length, protein accession, and protein length.
  • The columns are separated by tabs, so the table has seven columns.
  • The first column contains the gene ID, the second the taxon name, and the third the gene name (the "symbol").
  • Can you find the column with transcript accession numbers? What about protein length?
Great work! Click to unlock celebratory cat #2

docs.title: 🐞 Making a list of the longest sequences
docs.text:
Now we will use a Bash script to locate the longest FOXP2 transcript and corresponding protein for each species and save their accession numbers in a list. The accession numbers will let us identify these sequences and download them later.

📍 Since this is a large script, it's safer to save it as a file and then run it. Create a new file:

nano list_longest.sh

Once your text editor is open, copy the script below and paste it into the editor using Ctrl+V. Don't be scared! The comments starting with # explain what each part of the script does.

# Removes the first line (header) from the file and passes the rest to the next command
tail -n +2 transcript_protein.tsv | \
# Extracts the first column (gene IDs)
cut -f1 | \
# Sorts gene IDs alphabetically and removes duplicates
sort -u | \
# Reads each unique gene ID one by one
while read GENE_IDS; do

        # Searches for lines where the first column matches the gene ID
        LONGEST=$(grep -w "^$GENE_IDS" transcript_protein.tsv | \
        # Sorts the filtered lines numerically (-n), in descending order (-r), based on column 7 (protein length)
        sort -t$'\t' -nr -k7 | \
        # Selects the top row (the transcript with the longest protein sequence)
        head -n1 | \
        # Extracts column 4 (transcript ID) and column 6 (protein ID)
        cut -f4,6 | \
        # Converts the tab-separated values into newline-separated values
        tr '\t' '\n');

        # Appends the transcript ID and protein ID of the longest transcript to longest.list
        printf "$LONGEST\n" >> longest.list;

done

Now run the script by entering bash list_longest.sh. This tells the terminal to interpret the file using Bash.

📍 After it runs successfully, your script should have created a file named longest.list. Let's take a look:

cat longest.list

You should see on your screen the accession numbers of the longest transcripts and proteins, like this:

docs.title: 🐞 Downloading the longest sequences
docs.text:
Finally, it's time to download the selected transcripts (your data set)! We will use the datasets download command to download the sequences from NCBI.

datasets download gene accession \
--inputfile longest.list \
--fasta-filter-file longest.list \
--include rna,cds,protein \
--filename longest.zip

After running this command, you should see output similar to this:

Collecting 10 gene records [================================================] 100% 10/10
Downloading: longest.zip    33.5kB valid zip structure -- files not checked
Validating package [================================================] 100% 7/7
If the progress bar reaches 100%, the download was successful. The result is a ZIP file called longest.zip.

📍 Now let's look at the downloaded sequences by unzipping longest.zip:

unzip longest.zip

After entering the command, you should see output similar to this:

Archive:  longest.zip
  inflating: README.md
  inflating: ncbi_dataset/data/rna.fna
  inflating: ncbi_dataset/data/cds.fna
  inflating: ncbi_dataset/data/protein.faa
  inflating: ncbi_dataset/data/data_report.jsonl
  inflating: ncbi_dataset/data/dataset_catalog.json
  inflating: md5sum.txt

Now, if you list (ls) what's inside your current folder, you will notice a new folder called ncbi_dataset. Let's see what's inside:

ls ncbi_dataset

Inside ncbi_dataset there's a folder called data. To see what's inside data, use ls again, followed by the path to data:

ls ncbi_dataset/data

You should see the following files: cds.fna data_report.jsonl dataset_catalog.json protein.faa rna.fna

🌺 And there's our data!

The sequence data of the FOXP2 gene is contained in 3 files:

  • rna.fna contains the selected transcripts.
  • protein.faa contains the corresponding protein sequences.
  • cds.fna (which will be important in the next tutorials) contains the coding sequences.

Using head, take a look at the first lines of these three files. But watch out! You are inside tutorial_3, and the files are in ncbi_dataset/data. There are two ways to run the command:

  • Navigate to data, then use head:
cd ncbi_dataset/data
head rna.fna
  • Run head from your current directory and provide the path to the input file:
head ncbi_dataset/data/rna.fna

Choose whichever way you prefer, and do this for all three files. The first lines of rna.fna should look like this:

>XM_015469121.3 FOXP2 [organism=Bos taurus] [GeneID=505502] [transcript=X1]

docs.title: 🍄 Editing the headers of a fasta file
docs.text:
The FASTA headers contain several fields. This command creates shorter headers from the gene name, organism, and transcript information, while leaving the sequence lines unchanged. It writes the result to cds_headers.fna.

awk -F' ' '
/^>/ {
    gene = $2                          # Extract second field (FOXP2)
    sub(/\[organism=/, "", $3)         # Remove "[organism=" from third field
    org = substr($3, 1, 1)             # Take the first letter (C)
    sub(/\]/, "", $4)                  # Remove closing bracket if present
    ending = substr($4, 1, 3)          # Take first three letters (lup)
    print ">" gene "_" org ending      # Output formatted header
    next                               # Skip further processing for header lines
}
{print}  # Print sequence lines unchanged
' cds.fna > cds_headers.fna

Yaay! You did it!

Your final output is the cds_headers.fna file. Remember this for tutorial 4. Also, don't forget to deactivate your ncbi_datasets environment by using one of these commands below:

conda deactivate
source deactivate

docs.title: 1. Why align sequences?
docs.text:
Once we have extracted the gene sequences from NCBI, we need to align them.

What does aligning mean?

Alignment arranges similar parts of sequences from different species so that we can compare them. In an alignment, each position is treated as descended from a common ancestral sequence.

🍄 There are many software programs for building multi-species alignments. Here we are going to learn about two popular ones: MAFFT and PRANK.

MAFFT is available online and from the command line, and we will learn how to use both. Then, we will also learn how to use PRANK from the command line.

docs.title: 🍄 Using MAFFT online
docs.text:
1. Open the MAFFT online server.
  2. Paste your entire sequence file into the text box, or upload it from your computer using Choose file.

  3. Select your output formatting options.

  4. Select an alignment strategy and any other advanced options.

    • For relatively small data sets (fewer than 200 sequences), E-INS-i, L-INS-i, or G-INS-i may be suitable.
    • If you are unsure which options to use, the defaults are a reasonable starting point.

  5. Select Submit.

  6. When the alignment is complete, the results page should have a FASTA button near the top. Select it to download the alignment in FASTA format, then save it in your tutorial_4 folder with a meaningful name, such as FOXP2_nuc_aligned_mafft.fasta.

docs.title: 🍄 Using MAFFT on command line
docs.text:
1. Navigate to your Tutorial 3 folder, then to the subfolder containing your FOXP2 sequences:

    cd tutorial_3/ncbi_dataset/data/

  2. Copy your coding sequence file - the final output from tutorial 3(cds_headers.fna) from the Tutorial 3 folder to the Tutorial 4 folder:

    cp cds_headers.fna _ ../../../tutorial_4/

  3. Navigate to your Tutorial 4 folder and list its contents to check that the files were copied:

    cd ../../../tutorial_4
ls

    You should now see your sequence files in the folder.

    If you have mafft in a conda environment

    Activate the conda environment where MAFFT is installed using one of the commands below. MAFFT will not be available until you activate it.

        source activate mafft
    conda activate mafft

  4. Run MAFFT using a command with this format:

    mafft [options] input.fasta > output.fasta

    🐞 Let's break down the command:

    • [options] are the MAFFT settings you can choose. See the MAFFT manual for the full list.
    • input.fasta is the name or path to your unaligned sequence file.
    • output.fasta is the name or path for the output alignment.

    Here's an example command:

    mafft --nuc --globalpair --maxiterate 1000 --inputorder cds_headers.fna > FOXP2_nuc_aligned_mafft.fasta

    cds.fna is the unaligned sequence file downloaded from NCBI. FOXP2_nuc_aligned_mafft.fasta is an example output name; you can choose another name, but keep the .fasta extension.

🐞 Want to build your own command?

  1. Read the MAFFT manual to learn what the options in the example command do.
  2. Choose your own options, as you did for the online version, and build a MAFFT command.
  3. Run your command in the terminal and watch the magic happen!

docs.title: 🍄 Using PRANK on command line
docs.text:
1. In your terminal, make sure you are logged in to your lab's server.

  2. Activate the PRANK environment:

    source activate prank

  3. Run PRANK with a command like this, replacing the input and output names with your own:

    prank -d=input.fasta -o=output -F

    🐞 Let's break down this command:

    • -d specifies the input data file.
    • -o specifies the output name or path.
    • -F is an option recommended by the manual to avoid ignoring gaps and insertions.

  4. View the resulting alignment in the terminal using cat and the output file name.

docs.title: 4. Visualizing alignments
docs.text:
There are many programs for viewing and editing multi-species alignments. You can find a list of alignment viewers here.

Many alignment viewers have similar options, so feel free to choose the one that best suits your preferences.

docs.title: 🍄 Using AliView to visualize alignments
docs.text: 1. Open AliView, select File > Open file, and navigate to the alignment you want to view.

docs.title: 🍄 Removing stop codons from an alignment
docs.text:
Use seqkit mutate to remove the stop codons TAA, TAG, and TGA from an alignment:

seqkit mutate -i -p "TAA|TAG|TGA" -r "" alignment.fasta > alignment_no_stops.fasta

docs.title: Tutorial 5 - Estimating gene trees with IQTree
🌺 What are gene trees?
docs.text:
Gene trees, like other phylogenetic trees, represent a hypothesis about the evolutionary history of a group of organisms. While species trees may be inferred using many genes and other evidence, a gene tree is inferred from an alignment of one gene.

Gene trees and species trees

A gene tree represents the evolutionary history of a particular gene. It may therefore differ from a species tree, which represents the evolutionary history of the species.

📍 Similarly, we can use a protein alignment to make a protein tree, or a codon alignment to make a codon tree.

docs.title: 🍄 IQ-TREE: a program to estimate phylogenetic trees
docs.text:
One popular program for estimating phylogenetic trees is IQ-TREE.

IQ-TREE can estimate gene, protein, and codon trees. These trees can help us understand the evolutionary history represented by a sequence alignment and can be used as input for evolutionary models.

📍 IQ-TREE has both a web version and a command-line version. Let's learn how to use both.

docs.title: 🌺 Using IQ-TREE web version
docs.text:
1. Open the IQ-TREE web server.
  2. Read the IQ-TREE web server tutorial.
  3. Use Browse to select your sequence alignment file.

  4. Choose your analysis options:

    • Under Sequence type, select the type of alignment you have: DNA (nucleotides), codon, or protein.

    • Under Substitution model, leave the default Auto option to let IQ-TREE select a suitable substitution model for your data.

    • Under Branch Support Model, select None for bootstrap analysis and No for the SH-aLRT branch test. These tests provide statistical support for the tree topology; if you only want to inspect the topology, you can leave them off.

  5. Optionally, enter your email address if you would like to receive a notification, then select Submit.

  6. Open the Analysis Results tab to check the status of your job. When the status is Success, select the checkbox beside the job and choose Download selected jobs.

docs.title: 🌺 Using IQ-TREE on the command line
docs.text:
1. Navigate to the folder containing your sequence alignments. You can use nucleotide, protein, or codon alignments as input.

  2. If your IQtree is in a conda environment, activate the IQ-TREE environment using one of these:

    source activate iqtree
conda activate iqtree

  3. Run IQ-TREE with a command like this, replacing the placeholders with settings for your data:

    iqtree -s sequence_alignment -st sequence_type -m model -pre output_file_prefix -nt number_threads

    The options are:

    • -s specifies the path to your sequence alignment.
    • -st specifies the sequence type: DNA, AA, or CODON.
    • -m selects the model IQ-TREE uses to estimate the tree. To let IQ-TREE select a model, use -m TEST or -m MFP.
    • -pre sets the prefix for the output files. You do not need to specify a file extension because IQ-TREE creates several output files with different extensions.
    • -nt specifies the number of CPU cores to use. You can use -nt AUTO to let IQ-TREE choose a number of cores.

    Here is an example command:

    iqtree -s FOXP2_nuc_aligned.fasta -st DNA -m MFP -pre FOXP2 -nt AUTO

    📍 For more information about command-line options, see the IQ-TREE command reference.

  4. After IQ-TREE finishes, list the output files with ls FOXP2*. This lists files whose names start with FOXP2.

  5. Find the file ending in .treefile and download it to your computer using scp or FileZilla. This is the main result: it contains the phylogenetic tree estimated by IQ-TREE.

📍 Now let's look at your tree.

docs.title: Tutorial 6 - Natural selection analyses with codeml
🌺 What are evolutionary models?
docs.text:
In the previous tutorials, we learned how to:

  • Extract genomic sequences from online databases.
  • Make sequence alignments.
  • Estimate gene trees.

Now, we are going to use our sequence alignments and gene trees as input for an evolutionary model using a program called codeml.

What is a model?

A model is a representation of a process—in our case, the evolutionary process. Codeml models are mathematical representations of how genomic sequences evolve.

docs.title: 🍂 Why are evolutionary models important?
docs.text:
We use evolutionary models to ask questions and test hypotheses about how a genomic sequence changed through time. For example:

  • Did brain genes evolve differently in humans than in other animals?
  • Which genes are evolving faster in our genome?
  • Which genes or non-coding sequences are associated with adaptations in marine mammals?

docs.title: 🌺 How do we measure evolution on a sequence?
docs.text:
There are many ways to represent evolution mathematically in a model. In molecular evolution (the study of genes, proteins, and related molecules), one popular measure is the omega ratio, or ω.

The omega ratio

ω measures natural selection acting on a sequence. It indicates the relative rates of nonsynonymous and synonymous substitutions, and is used to infer patterns of selection.

See the infographic below for a brief explanation of the ω ratio, and read these slides for more details.

docs.title: 🌺 What is codeml?
docs.text:
• Codeml is a program for running evolutionary models, particularly models of codon and amino acid substitution.
  • Codeml models use the ω ratio to estimate how codon or protein sequences changed through time and across different lineages.

docs.title: 🍂 What can we do with codeml?
docs.text:
We can use codeml for two main purposes: hypothesis testing and model fitting.

  • Hypothesis testing: We compare an alternative hypothesis (a possible explanation for patterns in the data) with a null hypothesis (a model without the proposed effect). Codeml can help us test whether the data provide evidence against the null hypothesis.
  • Model fitting: We use the sequences and trees to estimate parameters and learn about the evolutionary process, without starting from a specific hypothesis.

When results support an alternative hypothesis, codeml can also help identify which parts of a gene may be evolving in a particular way.

Learn more about PAML and codeml

Codeml is part of PAML, a package that includes other programs. Learn more on the PAML website or in the PAML manual.

Recommended readings, from beginner to advanced:

  • Beginner's Guide on the Use of PAML to Detect Positive Selection
  • Adaptive Molecular Evolution: Detection Methods
  • Detecting the Signatures of Adaptive Evolution in Protein-Coding Genes
  • Inference of Episodic Changes in Natural Selection Acting on Protein Coding Sequences via CODEML

docs.title: 🍂 What types of models does codeml have?
docs.text:
Codeml has three types of models: branch models, site models and branch-site models.

  • Branch models allow ω to vary among branches. They can test whether some lineages in a phylogenetic tree evolved differently from others.

    For example: I wonder if whales evolved differently from other mammals.

  • Site models allow ω to vary among codons (sites). They can test whether some sites in a sequence evolved differently from the rest, or under positive selection.

    For example: Which codons in this virus genome are evolving faster, and could that help explain how the virus is adapting to a vaccine?

  • Branch-site models allow ω to vary among both branches and sites. They can test whether particular sites on specific branches evolved differently, or under positive selection.

    For example: I found evidence that whales evolved differently from other mammals. Which sites in these whale genes evolved faster?

docs.title: 🌺 Running codeml on command-line
docs.text: Before we begin, log in to your lab server. See Tutorial 2 for instructions. To run codeml, we first need a codon alignment and a codon tree.

docs.title: 🍂 Creating a codon alignment
docs.text:
To generate a codon alignment, we will use PRANK to process the FOXP2 nucleotide alignment created with MAFFT in Tutorial 4.

  1. Activate the PRANK environment:

    source activate prank

  2. Run PRANK using this command, replacing the input and output names with your own:

    prank -d=input.fasta -o=output_name -codon -F

    Replace input.fasta with the name or path to your nucleotide alignment, and replace output_name with the name you want for the output file. No extension is needed.

    For example:

    prank -d=FOXP2_nuc_aligned.fasta -o=FOXP2_codon_aligned -codon -F

  3. Convert the alignment format

    Codeml requires an alignment in PAML format, which is a modified PHYLIP format. To convert your codon alignment, use PRANK with the -convert option:

    prank -convert -d=alignment_codon.fas -f=paml -o=output_file_name -keep

docs.title: 🍂 Creating a codon tree
docs.text:
Now that we have a codon alignment, we can use IQ-TREE to generate a codon tree on the server.

  1. Activate the IQ-TREE environment:

    source activate iqtree

  2. Run IQ-TREE, replacing the alignment name and output prefix with your own. For the sequence type (-st), use CODON:

    iqtree -s sequence_alignment -st CODON -m MFP -pre output_file_prefix -nt AUTO

For more details about running IQ-TREE, see Tutorial 5.

docs.title: 🍂 Preparing your input files
docs.text:
Use codon input files

You must use a codon alignment and a codon tree. Codeml will not run with a DNA or protein alignment.

  1. Create a master folder for your codeml analyses. You can name it something other than codeml if you prefer:

    mkdir codeml

  2. Create a folder for this codeml run. We will start with model M0:

    mkdir codeml_M0

  3. Find the codon alignment and codon tree for the FOXP2 gene on your server.

  4. Use mv to move the alignment and tree files into your codeml_M0 folder. Replace the placeholders with your file paths:

    mv path/to/file/to/move path/to/destination

docs.title: 🍂 Writing the control file
docs.text:
We're almost there! Now we need to write the codeml control file. 😄

What is the control file?

The control file is a text document where you specify options for codeml. It tells codeml which model to run, where to find the input files, where to write the output, and which parameters to use.

The codeml control file looks like this:

seqfile = Mx_aln.phy                    * Path to the alignment file
treefile = Mx_unroot.tree               * Path to the tree file
outfile = out_M0.txt                    * Path to the output file
noisy = 3                               * Display moderate information on the screen
verbose = 1                             * Detailed output file
seqtype = 1                             * Codon data
ndata = 1                               * One gene alignment
icode = 0                               * Universal genetic code
cleandata = 0                           * Do not remove sites with ambiguity data
model = 0                               * One ω for all branches (M0 and site models)
NSsites = 0                             * One ω for all sites (M0 and branch model)
CodonFreq = 2                           * Use F3x4 model
clock = 0                               * Assume no clock
fix_omega = 0                           * Enables option to estimate omega
omega = 0.5                             * Initial omega value

Each line contains a codeml option, its value, and a comment after *. Codeml ignores the comments; they explain what the options mean.

The control file has many options, but you can think of them as settings for fine-tuning the model. In this tutorial, we will focus on six options:

Essential options for codeml beginners

seqfile — the name or path to your codon alignment. treefile — the name or path to your codon tree. outfile — the name for your codeml output file. model — the branch model to run. NSsites — the site model to run. omega — the initial omega value.

Now let's configure the control file for model M0 by setting these options.

docs.title: 🍁 Setting up the control file for the M0 model
docs.text:
1. What is the M0 model?

  • The M0 model is a basic codeml model, often used as a null hypothesis or to explore a data set.
  • M0 is also called the "one-ratio" model because it estimates one ω ratio across all branches and sites in the phylogenetic tree. It assumes that all lineages and codons evolve at the same rate.
  • This assumption may be too simple for some data sets. However, models are simplified representations of real-world processes, and M0 may fit some data well.
  • M0 can serve as a null hypothesis for comparison with more complex models.
  • Its estimated ω provides a baseline summary across sites and lineages.

2. Set up the M0 control file

To specify the M0 model, write the following options in your control file:

seqfile = name_sequence.phy             * Name or path to the alignment file
treefile = name_tree.tree               * Name or path to the tree file
outfile = out_M0.txt                    * Name or path to the output file
model = 0                               * One ω for all branches (M0 and site models)
NSsites = 0                             * One ω for all sites (M0 and branch model)
omega = 0.5                             * Initial omega value

docs.title: 🍂 Running codeml
docs.text:
1. Activate the PAML environment:

    source activate paml

  2. Run codeml, replacing control_file.ctl with the name of your control file:

    codeml control_file.ctl
